Quadtree — == Image processing using quadtrees == Quadtrees, particularly the region quadtree, have lent themselves well to image processing applications.
Quadtree — We will limit our discussion to binary image data, though region quadtrees and the image processing operations performed on them are just as suitable for colour images.
Quadtree — === Image union / intersection === One of the advantages of using quadtrees for image manipulation is that the set operations of union and intersection can be done simply and quickly.
Quadtree — Given two binary images, the image union (also called overlay) produces an image wherein a pixel is black if either of the input images has a black pixel in the same location.
Quadtree — That is, a pixel in the output image is white only when the corresponding pixel in both input images is white, otherwise the output pixel is black.
Quadtree — Rather than do the operation pixel by pixel, we can compute the union more efficiently by leveraging the quadtree's ability to represent multiple pixels with a single node.
Quadtree — For the purposes of discussion below, if a subtree contains both black and white pixels we will say that the root of that subtree is coloured grey.
Quadtree — The algorithm works by traversing the two input quadtrees ( T 1 {\displaystyle T_{1}} and T 2 {\displaystyle T_{2}} ) while building the output quadtree T {\displaystyle T} .
Quadtree — Consider the nodes v 1 ∈ T 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}\in T_{1}} and v 2 ∈ T 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}\in T_{2}} corresponding to the same region in the images.
Quadtree — If v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} or v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} is black, the corresponding node is created in T {\displaystyle T} and is colored black.
Quadtree — If only one of them is black and the other is gray, the gray node will contain a subtree underneath.
Quadtree — If v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} (respectively, v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} ) is white, v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} (respectively, v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} ) and the subtree underneath it (if any) is copied to T {\displaystyle T} .
Quadtree — If both v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} and v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} are gray, then the corresponding children of v 1 {\displaystyle v_{1}} and v 2 {\displaystyle v_{2}} are considered.
Quadtree — While this algorithm works, it does not by itself guarantee a minimally sized quadtree.
Quadtree — For example, consider the result if we were to union a checkerboard (where every tile is a pixel) of size 2 k × 2 k {\displaystyle 2^{k}\times 2^{k}} with its complement.
Quadtree — The result is a giant black square which should be represented by a quadtree with just the root node (coloured black), but instead the algorithm produces a full 4-ary tree of depth k {\displaystyle k} .
Quadtree — To fix this, we perform a bottom-up traversal of the resulting quadtree where we check if the four children nodes have the same colour, in which case we replace their parent with a leaf of the same colour.
Quadtree — One way to think about the intersection of the two images is that we are doing a union with respect to the white pixels.
Quadtree — As such, to perform the intersection we swap the mentions of black and white in the union algorithm.
Quadtree — === Connected component labelling === Consider two neighbouring black pixels in a binary image.
Quadtree — In general, two black pixels are connected if one can be reached from the other by moving only to adjacent pixels (i.e. there is a path of black pixels between them where each consecutive pair is adjacent).
Quadtree — Using the quadtree representation of images, Samet showed how we can find and label these connected components in time proportional to the size of the quadtree.
Quadtree — establish the adjacency relationships between black pixels process the equivalence relations from the first step to obtain one unique label for each connected component label the black pixels with the label associated with their connected component To simplify the discussion, let us assume the children of a node in the quadtree follow the Z-order (SW, NW, SE, NE).
Quadtree — Since we can count on this structure, for any cell we know how to navigate the quadtree to find the adjacent cells in the different levels of the hierarchy.
Quadtree — For each black leaf v {\displaystyle v} we look at the node or nodes representing cells that are Northern neighbours and Eastern neighbours (i.e. the Northern and Eastern cells that share edges with the cell of v {\displaystyle v} ).
Quadtree — Since the tree is organized in Z-order, we have the invariant that the Southern and Western neighbours have already been taken care of and accounted for.
Quadtree — Let the Northern or Eastern neighbour currently under consideration be u {\displaystyle u} .
Quadtree — If only one of u {\displaystyle u} or v {\displaystyle v} has a label, assign that label to the other cell If neither of them have labels, create one and assign it to both of them If u {\displaystyle u} and v {\displaystyle v} have different labels, record this label equivalence and move on Step two can be accomplished using the union-find data structure.
Quadtree — For every equivalence relation noted in the first step, we union the corresponding sets.
Quadtree — Afterwards, each distinct remaining set will be associated with a distinct connected component in the image.
Quadtree — This time, for each black node v {\displaystyle v} we use the union-find's find operation (with the old label of v {\displaystyle v} ) to find and assign v {\displaystyle v} its new label (associated with the connected component of which v {\displaystyle v} is part).
Quadtree — == Mesh generation using quadtrees == This section summarizes a chapter from a book by Har-Peled and de Berg et al.
Quadtree — Mesh generation is essentially the triangulation of a point set for which further processing may be performed.
Quadtree — As such, it is desirable for the resulting triangulation to have certain properties (like non-uniformity, triangles that are not "too skinny", large triangles in sparse areas and small triangles in dense ones, etc.) to make further processing quicker and less error-prone.
Quadtree — Quadtrees built on the point set can be used to create meshes with these desired properties.
Quadtree — Consider a leaf of the quadtree and its corresponding cell v {\displaystyle v} .
Quadtree — We say v {\displaystyle v} is balanced (for mesh generation) if the cell's sides are intersected by the corner points of neighbouring cells at most once on each side.
Quadtree — This means that the quadtree levels of leaves adjacent to v {\displaystyle v} differ by at most one from the level of v {\displaystyle v} .
Quadtree — When this is true for all leaves, we say the whole quadtree is balanced (for mesh generation).
Quadtree — Consider the cell v {\displaystyle v} and the 5 × 5 {\displaystyle 5\times 5} neighbourhood of same-sized cells centred at v {\displaystyle v} .
Quadtree — We say the quadtree is well-balanced if it is balanced, and for every leaf u {\displaystyle u} that contains a point of the point set, its extended cluster is also in the quadtree and the extended cluster contains no other point of the point set.
Quadtree — For every leaf, if there is a neighbour that is too large, subdivide the neighbour.
Quadtree — We also make sure that for a leaf with a point in it, the nodes for each leaf's extended cluster are in the tree.
Quadtree — For every leaf node v {\displaystyle v} that contains a point, if the extended cluster contains another point, we further subdivide the tree and rebalance as necessary.
Quadtree — If we needed to subdivide, for each child u {\displaystyle u} of v {\displaystyle v} we ensure the nodes of u {\displaystyle u} 's extended cluster are in the tree (and re-balance as required).
Quadtree — We consider the corner points of the tree cells as vertices in our triangulation.
Quadtree — Before the transformation step we have a bunch of boxes with points in some of them.
Quadtree — The transformation step is done in the following manner: for each point, warp the closest corner of its cell to meet it and triangulate the resulting four quadrangles to make "nice" triangles (the interested reader is referred to chapter 12 of Har-Peled for more details on what makes "nice" triangles).
Quadtree — For each regular square (no points within and no corner points in its sides), introduce the diagonal.
Quadtree — Due to the way in which we separated points with the well-balancing property, no square with a corner intersecting a side is one that was warped.
Quadtree — If there is one intersected side, the square becomes three triangles by adding the long diagonals connecting the intersection with opposite corners.
Quadtree — If there are four intersected sides, we split the square in half by adding an edge between two of the four intersections, and then connect these two endpoints to the remaining two intersection points.
Quadtree — For the other squares, we introduce a point in the middle and connect it to all four corners of the square as well as each intersection point.
Quadtree — At the end of it all, we have a nice triangulated mesh of our point set built from a quadtree.

R tree — R-trees are tree data structures used for spatial access methods, i.e., for indexing multi-dimensional information such as geographical coordinates, rectangles or polygons.
R tree — The R-tree was proposed by Antonin Guttman in 1984 and has found significant use in both theoretical and applied contexts.
R tree — A common real-world usage for an R-tree might be to store spatial objects such as restaurant locations or the polygons that typical maps are made of: streets, buildings, outlines of lakes, coastlines, etc. and then find answers quickly to queries such as "Find all museums within 2 km of my current location", "retrieve all road segments within 2 km of my location" (to display them in a navigation system) or "find the nearest gas station" (although not taking roads into account).
R tree — The R-tree can also accelerate nearest neighbor search for various distance metrics, including great-circle distance.
R tree — == R-tree idea == The key idea of the data structure is to group nearby objects and represent them with their minimum bounding rectangle in the next higher level of the tree; the "R" in R-tree is for rectangle.
R tree — Since all objects lie within this bounding rectangle, a query that does not intersect the bounding rectangle also cannot intersect any of the contained objects.
R tree — At the leaf level, each rectangle describes a single object; at higher levels the aggregation includes an increasing number of objects.
R tree — Similar to the B-tree, the R-tree is also a balanced search tree (so all leaf nodes are at the same depth), organizes the data in pages, and is designed for storage on disk (as used in databases).
R tree — Each page can contain a maximum number of entries, often denoted as M {\displaystyle M} .
R tree — It also guarantees a minimum fill (except for the root node), however best performance has been experienced with a minimum fill of 30%–40% of the maximum number of entries (B-trees guarantee 50% page fill, and B*-trees even 66%).
R tree — The reason for this is the more complex balancing required for spatial data as opposed to linear data stored in B-trees.
R tree — As with most trees, the searching algorithms (e.g., intersection, containment, nearest neighbor search) are rather simple.
R tree — The key idea is to use the bounding boxes to decide whether or not to search inside a subtree.
R tree — Like B-trees, R-trees are suitable for large data sets and databases, where nodes can be paged to memory when needed, and the whole tree cannot be kept in main memory.
R tree — Even if data can be fit in memory (or cached), the R-trees in most practical applications will usually provide performance advantages over naive check of all objects when the number of objects is more than few hundred or so.
R tree — However, for in-memory applications, there are similar alternatives that can provide slightly better performance or be simpler to implement in practice.
R tree — To maintain in-memory computing for R-tree in a computer cluster where computing nodes are connected by a network, researchers have used RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) to implement data-intensive applications under R-tree in a distributed environment.
R tree — This approach is scalable for increasingly large applications and achieves high throughput and low latency performance for R-tree.
R tree — The key difficulty of R-tree is to build an efficient tree that on one hand is balanced (so the leaf nodes are at the same height) on the other hand the rectangles do not cover too much empty space and do not overlap too much (so that during search, fewer subtrees need to be processed).
R tree — For example, the original idea for inserting elements to obtain an efficient tree is to always insert into the subtree that requires least enlargement of its bounding box.
R tree — Once that page is full, the data is split into two sets that should cover the minimal area each.
R tree — Most of the research and improvements for R-trees aims at improving the way the tree is built and can be grouped into two objectives: building an efficient tree from scratch (known as bulk-loading) and performing changes on an existing tree (insertion and deletion).
R tree — R-trees do not guarantee good worst-case performance, but generally perform well with real-world data.
R tree — The (bulk-loaded) Priority R-tree variant of the R-tree is worst-case optimal, but due to its increased complexity it has remained confined to theoretical study and has not received much attention in practical applications.
R tree — When data is organized in an R-tree, the neighbors within a given distance r and the k nearest neighbors (for any Lp-Norm) of all points can efficiently be computed using a spatial join.
R tree — This is beneficial for many algorithms based on such queries, for example the Local Outlier Factor.
R tree — DeLi-Clu, Density-Link-Clustering is a cluster analysis algorithm that uses the R-tree structure for a similar kind of spatial join to efficiently compute an OPTICS clustering.
R tree — === Data layout === Data in R-trees is organized in pages that can have a variable number of entries (up to some pre-defined maximum, and usually above a minimum fill).
R tree — Each entry within a non-leaf node stores two pieces of data: a way of identifying a child node, and the bounding box of all entries within this child node.
R tree — Leaf nodes store the data required for each child, often a point or bounding box representing the child and an external identifier for the child.
R tree — For polygon data (that often requires the storage of large polygons) the common setup is to store only the MBR (minimum bounding rectangle) of the polygon along with a unique identifier in the tree.
R tree — === Search === The search process in an R-tree embodies a two-phase approach that aligns with the Filter and Refine Principle (FRP).
R tree — In this structure, the internal nodes serve as an initial filter by quickly excluding regions of space that do not intersect the query, while the leaf nodes provide a refined, precise evaluation by storing the actual spatial objects.
R tree — Every internal node contains a set of rectangles and pointers to the corresponding child node and every leaf node contains the rectangles of spatial objects (the pointer to some spatial object can be there).
R tree — For every rectangle in a node, it has to be decided if it overlaps the search rectangle or not.
R tree — Searching is done like this in a recursive manner until all overlapping nodes have been traversed.
R tree — When a leaf node is reached, the contained bounding boxes (rectangles) are tested against the search rectangle and their objects (if there are any) are put into the result set if they lie within the search rectangle.
R tree — For priority search such as nearest neighbor search, the query consists of a point or rectangle.
R tree — Until the queue is empty or the desired number of results have been returned the search continues by processing the nearest entry in the queue.
R tree — This approach can be used with various distance metrics, including great-circle distance for geographic data.
R tree — === Insertion === To insert an object, the tree is traversed recursively from the root node.
R tree — At each step, all rectangles in the current directory node are examined, and a candidate is chosen using a heuristic such as choosing the rectangle which requires least enlargement.
R tree — Again, since an exhaustive search is too expensive, a heuristic is employed to split the node into two.
R tree — Adding the newly created node to the previous level, this level can again overflow, and these overflows can propagate up to the root node; when this node also overflows, a new root node is created and the tree has increased in height.
R tree — ==== Choosing the insertion subtree ==== The algorithm needs to decide in which subtree to insert.
R tree — When a data object is fully contained in a single rectangle, the choice is clear.
R tree — When there are multiple options or rectangles in need of enlargement, the choice can have a significant impact on the performance of the tree.
R tree — What happens next is it tries to minimize the overlap (in case of ties, prefer least enlargement and then least area); at the higher levels, it behaves similar to the R-tree, but on ties again preferring the subtree with smaller area.
R tree — The decreased overlap of rectangles in the R*-tree is one of the key benefits over the traditional R-tree.
R tree — ==== Splitting an overflowing node ==== Since redistributing all objects of a node into two nodes has an exponential number of options, a heuristic needs to be employed to find the best split.
R tree — In the classic R-tree, Guttman proposed two such heuristics, called QuadraticSplit and LinearSplit.
R tree — In quadratic split, the algorithm searches for the pair of rectangles that is the worst combination to have in the same node, and puts them as initial objects into the two new groups.
R tree — It then searches for the entry which has the strongest preference for one of the groups (in terms of area increase) and assigns the object to this group until all objects are assigned (satisfying the minimum fill).
R tree — There are other splitting strategies such as Greene's Split, the R*-tree splitting heuristic (which again tries to minimize overlap, but also prefers quadratic pages) or the linear split algorithm proposed by Ang and Tan (which however can produce very irregular rectangles, which are less performant for many real world range and window queries).
R tree — In addition to having a more advanced splitting heuristic, the R*-tree also tries to avoid splitting a node by reinserting some of the node members, which is similar to the way a B-tree balances overflowing nodes.
R tree — Finally, the X-tree can be seen as a R*-tree variant that can also decide to not split a node, but construct a so-called super-node containing all the extra entries, when it doesn't find a good split (in particular for high-dimensional data).
R tree — === Deletion === Deleting an entry from a page may require updating the bounding rectangles of parent pages.
R tree — Instead, the page will be dissolved and all its children (which may be subtrees, not only leaf objects) will be reinserted.
R tree — If during this process the root node has a single element, the tree height can decrease.
R tree — === Bulk-loading === Nearest-X: Objects are sorted by their first coordinate ("X") and then split into pages of the desired size.
R tree — Packed Hilbert R-tree: variation of Nearest-X, but sorting using the Hilbert value of the center of a rectangle instead of using the X coordinate.
R tree — Sort-Tile-Recursive (STR): Another variation of Nearest-X, that estimates the total number of leaves required as l = ⌈ number of objects / capacity ⌉ {\displaystyle l=\lceil {\text{number of objects}}/{\text{capacity}}\rceil } , the required split factor in each dimension to achieve this as s = ⌈ l 1 / d ⌉ {\displaystyle s=\lceil l^{1/d}\rceil } , then repeatedly splits each dimensions successively into s {\displaystyle s} equal sized partitions using 1-dimensional sorting.
R tree — The resulting pages, if they occupy more than one page, are again bulk-loaded using the same algorithm.
R tree — For point data, the leaf nodes will not overlap, and "tile" the data space into approximately equal sized pages.
R tree — Overlap Minimizing Top-down (OMT): Improvement over STR using a top-down approach which minimizes overlaps between slices and improves query performance.
R tree — == See also == Segment tree Interval tree – A degenerate R-tree for one dimension (usually time).
Frustum culling — In 3D computer graphics, hidden-surface determination (also known as shown-surface determination, hidden-surface removal (HSR), occlusion culling (OC) or visible-surface determination (VSD)) is the process of identifying what surfaces and parts of surfaces can be seen from a particular viewing angle.
Frustum culling — A hidden-surface determination algorithm is a solution to the visibility problem, which was one of the first major problems in the field of 3D computer graphics.
Frustum culling — The process of hidden-surface determination is sometimes called hiding, and such an algorithm is sometimes called a hider.
Frustum culling — Hidden-surface determination is necessary to render a scene correctly, so that one may not view features hidden behind the model itself, allowing only the naturally viewable portion of the graphic to be visible.
Frustum culling — == Background == Hidden-surface determination is a process that identifies which surfaces are not visible to the user (for example, because they lie behind opaque objects such as walls).
Frustum culling — Despite advances in hardware capability, rendering algorithms require substantial computational resources.
Frustum culling — By deciding that certain surfaces do not need to be rendered because they are not visible, rendering engines can improve efficiency, allowing the rendering of large world spaces.
Frustum culling — There are many techniques for hidden-surface determination, but they generally rely on sorting the surfaces based on their distance from the viewer.
Frustum culling — Sorting large quantities of graphics primitives can be computationally-expensive and is usually done by divide and conquer.
Frustum culling — The different hidden-surface determination techniques differ, in part, through the way in which the space is partitioned prior to sorting.
Frustum culling — == Algorithms == A rendering pipeline typically entails the following steps: projection, clipping, and rasterization.
Frustum culling — Z-buffering During rasterization, the depth (Z value) of each pixel (or sample in the case of anti-aliasing, but without loss of generality the term pixel is used) is checked against an existing depth value.
Frustum culling — If the current pixel is behind the pixel in the Z-buffer, the pixel is rejected, otherwise, it is shaded and its depth value replaces the one in the Z-buffer.
Frustum culling — Z-buffering supports dynamic scenes easily and is currently implemented efficiently in graphics hardware.
Frustum culling — Z-buffering requires up to 4 bytes per pixel, and can have a substantial computational cost since the rasterization algorithm needs to check each rasterized sample against the Z-buffer.
Frustum culling — The Z-buffer algorithm can suffer from artifacts due to precision errors (also known as Z-fighting).
Frustum culling — Coverage buffers (C-buffer) and surface buffer (S-buffer) Faster than Z-buffering and commonly used in games such as Quake I, these approaches store information about already displayed segments for each line of the screen (in contrast of storing each pixel as is the case for Z-buffering).
Frustum culling — New polygons are then cut against already displayed segments that would hide them.
Frustum culling — An S-buffer can display unsorted polygons, while a C-buffer requires polygons to be displayed from the nearest to the furthest.
Frustum culling — Because the C-buffer technique does not require a pixel to be drawn more than once, the process is slightly faster.
Frustum culling — Sorted active edge list Used in Quake I, this technique stores a list of the edges of already displayed polygons (see scanline rendering).
Frustum culling — New polygons are clipped against already displayed polygons' edges, creating new polygons to display, then storing the additional edges.
Frustum culling — Such an approach is harder to implement than S/C/Z-buffers, but it scales much better with increased image resolution.
Frustum culling — Painter's algorithm This algorithm sorts polygons by their barycenter and draws them back to front.
Frustum culling — This approach produces few artifacts when applied to scenes with polygons of similar size forming smooth meshes and back-face culling turned on.
Frustum culling — The drawbacks are the computational cost of the sorting step and the fact that visual artifacts can occur.
Frustum culling — This algorithm can fail for general scenes, as it cannot handle polygons in various common configurations, such as surfaces that intersect each other.
Frustum culling — Binary space partitioning (BSP) This technique divides a scene along planes corresponding to polygon boundaries.
Frustum culling — The subdivision is constructed in such a way as to provide an unambiguous depth ordering from any point in the scene when the BSP tree is traversed.
Frustum culling — The main disadvantage of the technique is the high computational cost of the construction of the BSP tree.
Frustum culling — As a result, this approach is less suitable for scenes consisting of dynamic geometry.
Frustum culling — The advantage of BSP is that the data is pre-sorted and error-free, and can be used as input for the previously mentioned algorithms.
Frustum culling — Ray tracing Ray tracing attempts to model the path of light rays to a viewpoint by tracing rays from the viewpoint into the scene.
Frustum culling — Although not a hidden-surface removal algorithm as such, it implicitly solves the hidden-surface removal problem by finding the nearest surface along each view-ray.
Frustum culling — Effectively this approach is equivalent to sorting all the geometry on a per-pixel basis.
Frustum culling — The Warnock algorithm This algorithm divides the screen into smaller areas and sorts triangles within these.
Frustum culling — If there is ambiguity (i.e., polygons overlap in-depth extent within these areas), then further subdivision occurs.
Frustum culling — == Culling and visible-surface determination == A related area to visible-surface determination is culling, which usually happens before visible-surface determination in a rendering pipeline.
Frustum culling — Primitives or batches of primitives can be rejected in their entirety, which usually reduces the computational load in a rendering system.Types of culling algorithms include:
Frustum culling — === Viewing-frustum culling === The viewing frustum is a geometric representation of the volume visible to the virtual camera.
Frustum culling — Naturally, objects outside this volume will not be visible in the final image, so they are discarded.
Frustum culling — These objects are cut into pieces along this boundary in a process called clipping, and the pieces that lie outside the frustum are discarded as there is no place to draw them.
Frustum culling — With 3D objects, some of the object's surface is facing the camera, and the rest is facing away from the camera, i.e. is on the backside of the object, hindered by the front side.
Frustum culling — These surfaces are determined by the vertex winding order: if the triangle drawn has its vertices in clockwise order on the projection plane when facing the camera, they switch into counter-clockwise order when the surface turns away from the camera.
Frustum culling — Incidentally, this approach also makes the objects completely transparent when the viewpoint camera is located inside them, because then all the surfaces of the object are facing away from the camera and are culled by the renderer.
Frustum culling — To prevent this artifact, the object must be set as double-sided (i.e. no back-face culling is done) or have separate inside surfaces.
Frustum culling — === Contribution culling === Often, objects are so far away that they do not contribute significantly to the final image.
Frustum culling — This is a very popular mechanism to speed up the rendering of large scenes that have a moderate to high depth complexity.
Frustum culling — Potentially visible set (PVS) rendering divides a scene into regions and pre-computes visibility for them.
Frustum culling — These visibility sets are then indexed at run-time to obtain high-quality visibility sets (accounting for complex occluder interactions) quickly.
Frustum culling — Portal rendering divides a scene into cells/sectors (rooms) and portals (doors), and computes which sectors are visible by clipping them against portals.
Frustum culling — Hansong Zhang's dissertation "Effective Occlusion Culling for the Interactive Display of Arbitrary Models" describes an occlusion culling approach.
Frustum culling — == Divide and conquer == A popular theme in the visible surface determination literature is divide and conquer.
Frustum culling — Beam tracing is a ray-tracing approach that divides the visible volumes into beams.
Frustum culling — Various screen-space subdivision approaches reduce the number of primitives considered per region, e.g. tiling, or screen-space BSP clipping.
Frustum culling — Z-buffer hardware may typically include a coarse "hi-Z", against which primitives can be rejected early without rasterization.
Frustum culling — Bounding volume hierarchies (BVHs) are often used to subdivide the scene's space (examples are the BSP tree, the octree and the kd-tree).
Frustum culling — This approach allows visibility determination to be performed hierarchically: if a node in the tree is considered to be invisible, then all of its child nodes are also invisible, and no further processing is necessary (they can all be rejected by the renderer).
Frustum culling — If a node is considered visible, then each of its children needs to be evaluated.
Frustum culling — This traversal is effectively a tree walk, where invisibility/occlusion or reaching a leaf node determines whether to stop or whether to recurse, respectively.

Signed distance function — In mathematics and its applications, the signed distance function or signed distance field (SDF) is the orthogonal distance of a given point x to the boundary of a set Ω in a metric space (such as the surface of a geometric shape), with the sign determined by whether or not x is in the interior of Ω.
Signed distance function — The function has positive values at points x inside Ω, it decreases in value as x approaches the boundary of Ω where the signed distance function is zero, and it takes negative values outside of Ω.
Signed distance function — However, the alternative convention is also sometimes taken instead (i.e., negative inside Ω and positive outside).
Signed distance function — == Definition == Let Ω be a subset of a metric space X with metric d, and ∂ Ω {\displaystyle \partial \Omega } be its boundary.
Signed distance function — The distance between a point x of X and the subset ∂ Ω {\displaystyle \partial \Omega } of X is defined as usual as
Signed distance function — d ( x , ∂ Ω ) = inf y ∈ ∂ Ω d ( x , y ) , {\displaystyle d(x,\partial \Omega )=\inf _{y\in \partial \Omega }d(x,y),}
Signed distance function — The signed distance function from a point x of X to Ω {\displaystyle \Omega } is defined by
Signed distance function — f ( x ) = { d ( x , ∂ Ω ) if x ∈ Ω − d ( x , ∂ Ω ) if x ∉ Ω . {\displaystyle f(x)={\begin{cases}d(x,\partial \Omega )&{\text{if }}x\in \Omega \\-d(x,\partial \Omega )&{\text{if }}\,x\notin \Omega .\end{cases}}}
Signed distance function — == Properties in Euclidean space == If Ω is a subset of the Euclidean space Rn with piecewise smooth boundary, then the signed distance function is differentiable almost everywhere, and its gradient satisfies the eikonal equation
Signed distance function — If the boundary of Ω is Ck for k ≥ 2 (see Differentiability classes) then d is Ck on points sufficiently close to the boundary of Ω.
Signed distance function — The signed distance function is thus a differentiable extension of the normal vector field.
Signed distance function — In particular, the Hessian of the signed distance function on the boundary of Ω gives the Weingarten map.
Signed distance function — If, further, Γ is a region sufficiently close to the boundary of Ω that f is twice continuously differentiable on it, then there is an explicit formula involving the Weingarten map Wx for the Jacobian of changing variables in terms of the signed distance function and nearest boundary point.
Signed distance function — Specifically, if T(∂Ω, μ) is the set of points within distance μ of the boundary of Ω (i.e. the tubular neighbourhood of radius μ), and g is an absolutely integrable function on Γ, then
Signed distance function — ∫ T ( ∂ Ω , μ ) g ( x ) d x = ∫ ∂ Ω ∫ − μ μ g ( u + λ N ( u ) ) det ( I − λ W u ) d λ d S u , {\displaystyle \int _{T(\partial \Omega ,\mu )}g(x)\,dx=\int _{\partial \Omega }\int _{-\mu }^{\mu }g(u+\lambda N(u))\,\det(I-\lambda W_{u})\,d\lambda \,dS_{u},}
Signed distance function — where det denotes the determinant and dSu indicates that we are taking the surface integral.
Signed distance function — == Algorithms == Algorithms for calculating the signed distance function include the efficient fast marching method, fast sweeping method and the more general level-set method.
Signed distance function — For voxel rendering, a fast algorithm for calculating the SDF in taxicab geometry uses summed-area tables.
Signed distance function — Signed distance functions are applied, for example, in real-time rendering, for instance the method of SDF ray marching, and computer vision.
Signed distance function — SDF has been used to describe object geometry in real-time rendering, usually in a raymarching context, starting in the mid 2000s.
Signed distance function — By 2007, Valve is using SDFs to render large pixel-size (or high DPI) smooth fonts with GPU acceleration in its games.
Signed distance function — Valve's method is not perfect as it runs in raster space in order to avoid the computational complexity of solving the problem in the (continuous) vector space.
Signed distance function — Behdad's GLyphy approximates the font's Bézier curves with arc splines, accelerated by grid-based discretization techniques (which culls too-far-away points) to run in real time.
Signed distance function — A modified version of SDF was introduced as a loss function to minimise the error in interpenetration of pixels while rendering multiple objects.
Signed distance function — In particular, for any pixel that does not belong to an object, if it lies outside the object in rendition, no penalty is imposed; if it does, a positive value proportional to its distance inside the object is imposed.

Signed distance function — In 2020, the FOSS game engine Godot 4.0 received SDF-based real-time global illumination (SDFGI), that became a compromise between more realistic voxel-based GI and baked GI.
Signed distance function — Its core advantage is that it can be applied to infinite space, which allows developers to use it for open-world games.
Signed distance function — In 2023, the authors of the Zed text editor announced a GPUI framework that draws all UI elements using the GPU at 120 fps.
Signed distance function — The work makes use of Inigo Quilez's list of geometric primitives in SDF, Figma co-founder Evan Wallace's Gaussian blur in SDF, and a new rounded rectangle SDF.

Polygon mesh — In 3D computer graphics and solid modeling, a polygon mesh is a collection of vertices, edges and faces that defines the shape of a polyhedral object's surface.
Polygon mesh — The faces usually consist of triangles (triangle mesh), quadrilaterals (quads), or other simple convex polygons (n-gons).
Polygon mesh — A polygonal mesh may also be more generally composed of concave polygons, or even polygons with holes.
Polygon mesh — The study of polygon meshes is a large sub-field of computer graphics (specifically 3D computer graphics) and geometric modeling.
Polygon mesh — Different representations of polygon meshes are used for different applications and goals.
Polygon mesh — The variety of operations performed on meshes includes Boolean logic (Constructive solid geometry), smoothing, and simplification.
Polygon mesh — Algorithms also exist for ray tracing, collision detection, and rigid-body dynamics with polygon meshes.
Polygon mesh — If the mesh's edges are rendered instead of the faces, then the model becomes a wireframe model.
Polygon mesh — Several methods exist for mesh generation, including the marching cubes algorithm.
Polygon mesh — Volumetric meshes are distinct from polygon meshes in that they explicitly represent both the surface and interior region of a structure, while polygon meshes only explicitly represent the surface (the volume is implicit).
Polygon mesh — In many applications, only vertices, edges and either faces or polygons are stored.
Polygon mesh — A renderer may support only 3-sided faces, so polygons must be constructed of many of these, as shown above.
Polygon mesh — However, many renderers either support quads and higher-sided polygons, or are able to convert polygons to triangles on the fly, making it unnecessary to store a mesh in a triangulated form.
Polygon mesh — vertex A position (usually in 3D space) along with other information such as color, normal vector and texture coordinates. edge A connection between two vertices. face A closed set of edges, in which a triangle face has three edges, and a quad face has four edges.
Polygon mesh — However, most rendering hardware supports only 3- or 4-sided faces, so polygons are represented as multiple faces.
Polygon mesh — Mathematically, a polygonal mesh may be considered an unstructured grid, or undirected graph, with additional properties of geometry, shape and topology.
Polygon mesh — surfaces More often called smoothing groups, are useful, but not required to group smooth regions.
Polygon mesh — For smooth shading of the sides, all surface normals must point horizontally away from the center, while the normals of the caps must point straight up and down.
Polygon mesh — Rendered as a single, Phong-shaded surface, the crease vertices would have incorrect normals.
Polygon mesh — Thus, some way of determining where to cease smoothing is needed to group smooth parts of a mesh, just as polygons group 3-sided faces.
Polygon mesh — As an alternative to providing surfaces/smoothing groups, a mesh may contain other data for calculating the same data, such as a splitting angle (polygons with normals above this threshold are either automatically treated as separate smoothing groups or some technique such as splitting or chamfering is automatically applied to the edge between them.
Polygon mesh — Additionally, very high resolution meshes are less subject to issues that would require smoothing groups, as their polygons are so small as to make the need irrelevant.
Polygon mesh — Further, another alternative exists in the possibility of simply detaching the surfaces themselves from the rest of the mesh.
Polygon mesh — groups Some mesh formats contain groups, which define separate elements of the mesh, and are useful for determining separate sub-objects for skeletal animation or separate actors for non-skeletal animation.
Polygon mesh — materials Generally materials will be defined, allowing different portions of the mesh to use different shaders when rendered.
Polygon mesh — UV coordinates Most mesh formats also support some form of UV coordinates which are a separate 2d representation of the mesh "unfolded" to show what portion of a two-dimensional texture map to apply to different polygons of the mesh.
Polygon mesh — It is also possible for meshes to contain other such vertex attribute information such as colour, tangent vectors, weight maps to control animation, etc. (sometimes also called channels).
Polygon mesh — == Representations == Polygon meshes may be represented in a variety of ways, using different methods to store the vertex, edge and face data.
Polygon mesh — Face-vertex meshes A simple list of vertices, and a set of polygons that point to the vertices it uses.
Polygon mesh — Winged-edge in which each edge points to two vertices, two faces, and the four (clockwise and counterclockwise) edges that touch them.
Polygon mesh — Winged-edge meshes allow constant time traversal of the surface, but with higher storage requirements.
Polygon mesh — Half-edge meshes Similar to winged-edge meshes except that only half the edge traversal information is used. (see OpenMesh) Quad-edge meshes which store edges, half-edges, and vertices without any reference to polygons.
Polygon mesh — The polygons are implicit in the representation, and may be found by traversing the structure.
Polygon mesh — Corner-tables which store vertices in a predefined table, such that traversing the table implicitly defines polygons.
Polygon mesh — The representation is more compact, and more efficient for retrieving polygons, but operations to change polygons are slow.
Polygon mesh — Vertex-vertex meshesA VV mesh represents only vertices, which point to other vertices.
Polygon mesh — However, the simplicity of the representation does not allow for many efficient operations to be performed on meshes.
Polygon mesh — Each of the representations above have particular advantages and drawbacks, further discussed in Smith (2006).
Polygon mesh — The choice of the data structure is governed by the application, the performance required, size of the data, and the operations to be performed.
Polygon mesh — For example, it is easier to deal with triangles than general polygons, especially in computational geometry.
Polygon mesh — For certain operations it is necessary to have a fast access to topological information such as edges or neighboring faces; this requires more complex structures such as the winged-edge representation.
Polygon mesh — For hardware rendering, compact, simple structures are needed; thus the corner-table (triangle fan) is commonly incorporated into low-level rendering APIs such as DirectX and OpenGL.
Polygon mesh — Vertex-vertex meshes represent an object as a set of vertices connected to other vertices.
Polygon mesh — This is the simplest representation, but not widely used since the face and edge information is implicit.
Polygon mesh — Thus, it is necessary to traverse the data in order to generate a list of faces for rendering.
Polygon mesh — However, VV meshes benefit from small storage space and efficient morphing of shape.
Polygon mesh — The last two vertices, 8 and 9 at the top and bottom center of the "box-cylinder", have four connected vertices rather than five.
Polygon mesh — A general system must be able to handle an arbitrary number of vertices connected to any given vertex.
Polygon mesh — This is the most widely used mesh representation, being the input typically accepted by modern graphics hardware.
Polygon mesh — Face-vertex meshes improve on VV mesh for modeling in that they allow explicit lookup of the vertices of a face, and the faces surrounding a vertex.
Polygon mesh — Notice that, in this example, every face is required to have exactly 3 vertices.
Polygon mesh — However, this does not mean every vertex has the same number of surrounding faces.
Polygon mesh — For rendering, the face list is usually transmitted to the GPU as a set of indices to vertices, and the vertices are sent as position/color/normal structures (in the figure, only position is given).
Polygon mesh — This has the benefit that changes in shape, but not geometry, can be dynamically updated by simply resending the vertex data without updating the face connectivity.
Polygon mesh — Unlike VV meshes, both faces and vertices are explicit, so locating neighboring faces and vertices is constant time.
Polygon mesh — However, the edges are implicit, so a search is still needed to find all the faces surrounding a given face.
Polygon mesh — Other dynamic operations, such as splitting or merging a face, are also difficult with face-vertex meshes.
Polygon mesh — Introduced by Baumgart in 1975, winged-edge meshes explicitly represent the vertices, faces, and edges of a mesh.
Polygon mesh — This representation is widely used in modeling programs to provide the greatest flexibility in dynamically changing the mesh geometry, because split and merge operations can be done quickly.
Polygon mesh — Their primary drawback is large storage requirements and increased complexity due to maintaining many indices.
Polygon mesh — A good discussion of implementation issues of Winged-edge meshes may be found in the book Graphics Gems II.
Polygon mesh — Winged-edge meshes address the issue of traversing from edge to edge, and providing an ordered set of faces around an edge.
Polygon mesh — To simplify this, winged-edge meshes provide only four, the nearest clockwise and counter-clockwise edges at each end.
Polygon mesh — The information for each edge therefore resembles a butterfly, hence "winged-edge" meshes.
Polygon mesh — The total data for an edge consists of 2 vertices (endpoints), 2 faces (on each side), and 4 edges (winged-edge).
Polygon mesh — Rendering of winged-edge meshes for graphics hardware requires generating a Face index list, which is usually done only when the geometry changes.
Polygon mesh — Winged-edge meshes are ideally suited for dynamic geometry, such as subdivision surfaces and interactive modeling, since changes to the mesh can occur locally.
Polygon mesh — Traversal across the mesh, as might be needed for collision detection, can be accomplished efficiently.
Polygon mesh — === Render dynamic meshes === Winged-edge meshes are not the only representation which allows for dynamic changes to geometry.
Polygon mesh — A new representation which combines winged-edge meshes and face-vertex meshes is the render dynamic mesh, which explicitly stores both, the vertices of a face and faces of a vertex (like FV meshes), and the faces and vertices of an edge (like winged-edge).
Polygon mesh — Render dynamic meshes requires slightly less storage space than standard winged-edge meshes, and can be directly rendered by graphics hardware since the face list contains an index of vertices.
Polygon mesh — In addition, traversal from vertex to face is explicit (constant time), as is from face to vertex.
Polygon mesh — RD meshes do not require the four outgoing edges since these can be found by traversing from edge to face, then face to neighboring edge.
Polygon mesh — RD meshes benefit from the features of winged-edge meshes by allowing for geometry to be dynamically updated.
Polygon mesh — In the above table, explicit indicates that the operation can be performed in constant time, as the data is directly stored; list compare indicates that a list comparison between two lists must be performed to accomplish the operation; and pair search indicates a search must be done on two indices.
Polygon mesh — The notation avg(V,V) means the average number of vertices connected to a given vertex; avg(E,V) means the average number of edges connected to a given vertex, and avg(F,V) is the average number of faces connected to a given vertex.
Polygon mesh — The notation "V → f1, f2, f3, ... → v1, v2, v3, ..." describes that a traversal across multiple elements is required to perform the operation.
Polygon mesh — For example, to get "all vertices around a given vertex V" using the face-vertex mesh, it is necessary to first find the faces around the given vertex V using the vertex list.
Polygon mesh — Winged-edge meshes explicitly store nearly all information, and other operations always traverse to the edge first to get additional info.
Polygon mesh — Vertex-vertex meshes are the only representation that explicitly stores the neighboring vertices of a given vertex.
Polygon mesh — As the mesh representations become more complex (from left to right in the summary), the amount of information explicitly stored increases.
Polygon mesh — This gives more direct, constant time, access to traversal and topology of various elements but at the cost of increased overhead and space in maintaining indices properly.
Polygon mesh — Figure 7 shows the connectivity information for each of the four technique described in this article.
Polygon mesh — As a general rule, face-vertex meshes are used whenever an object must be rendered on graphics hardware that does not change geometry (connectivity), but may deform or morph shape (vertex positions) such as real-time rendering of static or morphing objects.
Polygon mesh — Winged-edge or render dynamic meshes are used when the geometry changes, such as in interactive modeling packages or for computing subdivision surfaces.
Polygon mesh — Vertex-vertex meshes are ideal for efficient, complex changes in geometry or topology so long as hardware rendering is not of concern.
Polygon mesh — == Other representations == Streaming meshes store faces in an ordered, yet independent, way so that the mesh can be transmitted in pieces.
Polygon mesh — The order of faces may be spatial, spectral, or based on other properties of the mesh.
Polygon mesh — Streaming meshes allow a very large mesh to be rendered even while it is still being loaded.
Polygon mesh — Progressive meshes transmit the vertex and face data with increasing levels of detail.
Polygon mesh — Unlike streaming meshes, progressive meshes give the overall shape of the entire object, but at a low level of detail.
Polygon mesh — Additional data, new edges and faces, progressively increase the detail of the mesh.
Polygon mesh — Normal meshes transmit progressive changes to a mesh as a set of normal displacements from a base mesh.
Polygon mesh — With this technique, a series of textures represent the desired incremental modifications.
Polygon mesh — Normal meshes are compact, since only a single scalar value is needed to express displacement.
Polygon mesh — However, the technique requires a complex series of transformations to create the displacement textures.
Polygon mesh — == File formats == There exist many different file formats for storing polygon mesh data.
Polygon mesh — Each format is most effective when used for the purpose intended by its creator.
