Neural radiance field — A neural radiance field (NeRF) is a neural field for reconstructing a three-dimensional representation of a scene from two-dimensional images.
Neural radiance field — The NeRF model enables downstream applications of novel view synthesis, scene geometry reconstruction, and obtaining the reflectance properties of the scene.
Neural radiance field — First introduced in 2020, it has since gained significant attention for its potential applications in computer graphics and content creation.
Neural radiance field — == Algorithm == The NeRF algorithm represents a scene as a radiance field parametrized by a deep neural network (DNN).
Neural radiance field — The network predicts a volume density and view-dependent emitted radiance given the spatial location ( x , y , z ) {\displaystyle (x,y,z)} and viewing direction in Euler angles ( θ , Φ ) {\displaystyle (\theta ,\Phi )} of the camera.
Neural radiance field — By sampling many points along camera rays, traditional volume rendering techniques can produce an image.
Neural radiance field — The first step is to collect images of the scene from different angles and their respective camera pose.
Neural radiance field — These images are standard 2D images and do not require a specialized camera or software.
Neural radiance field — Any camera is able to generate datasets, provided the settings and capture method meet the requirements for SfM (Structure from Motion).
Neural radiance field — This requires tracking of the camera position and orientation, often through some combination of SLAM, GPS, or inertial estimation.
Neural radiance field — For such data, images (rendered through traditional non-learned methods) and respective camera poses are reproducible and error-free.
Neural radiance field — === Training === For each sparse viewpoint (image and camera pose) provided, camera rays are marched through the scene, generating a set of 3D points with a given radiance direction (into the camera).
Neural radiance field — For these points, volume density and emitted radiance are predicted using the multi-layer perceptron (MLP).
Neural radiance field — Because this process is fully differentiable, the error between the predicted image and the original image can be minimized with gradient descent over multiple viewpoints, encouraging the MLP to develop a coherent model of the scene.
Neural radiance field — == Variations and improvements == Early versions of NeRF were slow to optimize and required that all input views were taken with the same camera in the same lighting conditions.
Neural radiance field — These performed best when limited to orbiting around individual objects, such as a drum set, plants or small toys.
Neural radiance field — Since the original paper in 2020, many improvements have been made to the NeRF algorithm, with variations for special use cases.
Neural radiance field — === Fourier feature mapping === In 2020, shortly after the release of NeRF, the addition of Fourier Feature Mapping improved training speed and image accuracy.
Neural radiance field — Deep neural networks struggle to learn high frequency functions in low dimensional domains; a phenomenon known as spectral bias.
Neural radiance field — To overcome this shortcoming, points are mapped to a higher dimensional feature space before being fed into the MLP.
Neural radiance field — γ ( v ) = [ a 1 cos ⁡ ( 2 π B 1 T v ) a 1 sin ⁡ ( 2 π B 1 T v ) ⋮ a m cos ⁡ ( 2 π B m T v ) a m sin ⁡ ( 2 π B m T v ) ] {\displaystyle \gamma (\mathrm {v} )={\begin{bmatrix}a_{1}\cos(2{\pi }{\mathrm {B} }_{1}^{T}\mathrm {v} )\\a_{1}\sin(2\pi {\mathrm {B} }_{1}^{T}\mathrm {v} )\\\vdots \\a_{m}\cos(2{\pi }{\mathrm {B} }_{m}^{T}\mathrm {v} )\\a_{m}\sin(2{\pi }{\mathrm {B} }_{m}^{T}\mathrm {v} )\end{bmatrix}}}
Neural radiance field — Where v {\displaystyle \mathrm {v} } is the input point, B i {\displaystyle \mathrm {B} _{i}} are the frequency vectors, and a i {\displaystyle a_{i}} are coefficients.
Neural radiance field — This allows for rapid convergence to high frequency functions, such as pixels in a detailed image.
Neural radiance field — === Bundle-adjusting neural radiance fields === One limitation of NeRFs is the requirement of knowing accurate camera poses to train the model.
Neural radiance field — Often times, pose estimation methods are not completely accurate, nor is the camera pose even possible to know.
Neural radiance field — So, a method was developed to optimize the camera pose along with the volumetric function itself.
Neural radiance field — Called Bundle-Adjusting Neural Radiance Field (BARF), the technique uses a dynamic low-pass filter (DLPF) to go from coarse to fine adjustment, minimizing error by finding the geometric transformation to the desired image.
Neural radiance field — This corrects imperfect camera poses and greatly improves the quality of NeRF renders.
Neural radiance field — === Multiscale representation === Conventional NeRFs struggle to represent detail at all viewing distances, producing blurry images up close and overly aliased images from distant views.
Neural radiance field — In 2021, researchers introduced a technique to improve the sharpness of details at different viewing scales known as mip-NeRF (comes from mipmap).
Neural radiance field — Rather than sampling a single ray per pixel, the technique fits a gaussian to the conical frustum cast by the camera.
Neural radiance field — This improvement effectively anti-aliases across all viewing scales. mip-NeRF also reduces overall image error and is faster to converge at about half the size of ray-based NeRF.
Neural radiance field — === Learned initializations === In 2021, researchers applied meta-learning to assign initial weights to the MLP.
Neural radiance field — This rapidly speeds up convergence by effectively giving the network a head start in gradient descent.
Neural radiance field — Meta-learning also allowed the MLP to learn an underlying representation of certain scene types.
Neural radiance field — For example, given a dataset of famous tourist landmarks, an initialized NeRF could partially reconstruct a scene given one image.
Neural radiance field — === NeRF in the wild === Conventional NeRFs are vulnerable to slight variations in input images (objects, lighting) often resulting in ghosting and artifacts.
Neural radiance field — As a result, NeRFs struggle to represent dynamic scenes, such as bustling city streets with changes in lighting and dynamic objects.
Neural radiance field — In 2021, researchers at Google developed a new method for accounting for these variations, named NeRF in the Wild (NeRF-W).
Neural radiance field — However, it operates in sequence with a separate MLP for appearance embedding (changes in lighting, camera properties) and an MLP for transient embedding (changes in scene objects).
Neural radiance field — This allows the NeRF to be trained on diverse photo collections, such as those taken by mobile phones at different times of day.
Neural radiance field — === Relighting === In 2021, researchers added more outputs to the MLP at the heart of NeRFs.
Neural radiance field — The output now included: volume density, surface normal, material parameters, distance to the first surface intersection (in any direction), and visibility of the external environment in any direction.
Neural radiance field — The inclusion of these new parameters lets the MLP learn material properties, rather than pure radiance values.
Neural radiance field — This facilitates a more complex rendering pipeline, calculating direct and global illumination, specular highlights, and shadows.
Neural radiance field — As a result, the NeRF can render the scene under any lighting conditions with no re-training.
Neural radiance field — === Plenoctrees === Although NeRFs had reached high levels of fidelity, their costly compute time made them useless for many applications requiring real-time rendering, such as VR/AR and interactive content.
Neural radiance field — Introduced in 2021, Plenoctrees (plenoptic octrees) enabled real-time rendering of pre-trained NeRFs through division of the volumetric radiance function into an octree.
Neural radiance field — Rather than assigning a radiance direction into the camera, viewing direction is taken out of the network input and spherical radiance is predicted for each region.
Neural radiance field — === Sparse Neural Radiance Grid === Similar to Plenoctrees, this method enabled real-time rendering of pretrained NeRFs.
Neural radiance field — To avoid querying the large MLP for each point, this method bakes NeRFs into Sparse Neural Radiance Grids (SNeRG).
Neural radiance field — A SNeRG is a sparse voxel grid containing opacity and color, with learned feature vectors to encode view-dependent information.
Neural radiance field — A lightweight, more efficient MLP is then used to produce view-dependent residuals to modify the color and opacity.
Neural radiance field — To enable this compressive baking, small changes to the NeRF architecture were made, such as running the MLP once per pixel rather than for each point along the ray.
Neural radiance field — === Instant NeRFs === In 2022, researchers at Nvidia enabled real-time training of NeRFs through a technique known as Instant Neural Graphics Primitives.
Neural radiance field — An innovative input encoding reduces computation, enabling real-time training of a NeRF, an improvement orders of magnitude above previous methods.
Neural radiance field — The speedup stems from the use of spatial hash functions, which have O ( 1 ) {\displaystyle O(1)} access times, and parallelized architectures which run fast on modern GPUs.
Neural radiance field — === Plenoxels === Plenoxel (plenoptic volume element) uses a sparse voxel representation instead of a volumetric approach as seen in NeRFs.
Neural radiance field — Plenoxel also completely removes the MLP, instead directly performing gradient descent on the voxel coefficients.
Neural radiance field — Plenoxel can match the fidelity of a conventional NeRF in orders of magnitude less training time.
Neural radiance field — Published in 2022, this method disproved the importance of the MLP, showing that the differentiable rendering pipeline is the critical component.
Neural radiance field — Gaussian splatting is a newer method that can outperform NeRF in render time and fidelity.
Neural radiance field — Rather than representing the scene as a volumetric function, it uses a sparse cloud of 3D gaussians.
Neural radiance field — First, a point cloud is generated (through structure from motion) and converted to gaussians of initial covariance, color, and opacity.
Neural radiance field — The gaussians are directly optimized through stochastic gradient descent to match the input image.
Neural radiance field — This saves computation by removing empty space and foregoing the need to query a neural network for each point.
Neural radiance field — Instead, simply "splat" all the gaussians onto the screen and they overlap to produce the desired image.
Neural radiance field — === Photogrammetry === Traditional photogrammetry is not neural, instead using robust geometric equations to obtain 3D measurements.
Neural radiance field — NeRFs, unlike photogrammetric methods, do not inherently produce dimensionally accurate 3D geometry.
Neural radiance field — While their results are often sufficient for extracting accurate geometry (ex: via cube marching), the process is fuzzy, as with most neural methods.
Neural radiance field — This limits NeRF to cases where the output image is valued, rather than raw scene geometry.
Neural radiance field — For example, photogrammetric methods completely break down when trying to reconstruct reflective or transparent objects in a scene, while a NeRF is able to infer the geometry.
Neural radiance field — == Applications == NeRFs have a wide range of applications, and are starting to grow in popularity as they become integrated into user-friendly applications.
Neural radiance field — === Content creation === NeRFs have huge potential in content creation, where on-demand photorealistic views are extremely valuable.
Neural radiance field — The technology democratizes a space previously only accessible by teams of VFX artists with expensive assets.
Neural radiance field — Neural radiance fields now allow anyone with a camera to create compelling 3D environments.
Neural radiance field — NeRF has been combined with generative AI, allowing users with no modelling experience to instruct changes in photorealistic 3D scenes.
Neural radiance field — NeRFs have potential uses in video production, computer graphics, and product design.
Neural radiance field — ==== Interactive content ==== The photorealism of NeRFs make them appealing for applications where immersion is important, such as virtual reality or videogames.
Neural radiance field — NeRFs can be combined with classical rendering techniques to insert synthetic objects and create believable virtual experiences.
Neural radiance field — === Medical imaging === NeRFs have been used to reconstruct 3D CT scans from sparse or even single X-ray views.
Neural radiance field — If adopted, this method can save patients from excess doses of ionizing radiation, allowing for safer diagnosis.
Neural radiance field — === Robotics and autonomy === The unique ability of NeRFs to understand transparent and reflective objects makes them useful for robots interacting in such environments.
Neural radiance field — The use of NeRF allowed a robot arm to precisely manipulate a transparent wine glass; a task where traditional computer vision would struggle.
Neural radiance field — NeRFs can also generate photorealistic human faces, making them valuable tools for human-computer interaction.
Neural radiance field — Traditionally rendered faces can be uncanny, while other neural methods are too slow to run in real-time.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is the computational problem of constructing or updating a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously keeping track of an agent's location within it.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — While this initially appears to be a chicken or the egg problem, there are several algorithms known to solve it in, at least approximately, tractable time for certain environments.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Popular approximate solution methods include the particle filter, extended Kalman filter, covariance intersection, and GraphSLAM.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — SLAM algorithms are based on concepts in computational geometry and computer vision, and are used in robot navigation, robotic mapping and odometry for virtual reality or augmented reality.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — SLAM algorithms are tailored to the available resources and are not aimed at perfection but at operational compliance.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Published approaches are employed in self-driving cars, unmanned aerial vehicles, autonomous underwater vehicles, planetary rovers, newer domestic robots and even inside the human body.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — == Mathematical description of the problem == Given a series of controls u t {\displaystyle u_{t}} and sensor observations o t {\displaystyle o_{t}} over discrete time steps t {\displaystyle t} , the SLAM problem is to compute an estimate of the agent's state x t {\displaystyle x_{t}} and a map of the environment m t {\displaystyle m_{t}} .
Simultaneous localization and mapping — P ( m t + 1 , x t + 1 | o 1 : t + 1 , u 1 : t ) {\displaystyle P(m_{t+1},x_{t+1}|o_{1:t+1},u_{1:t})}
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Applying Bayes' rule gives a framework for sequentially updating the location posteriors, given a map and a transition function P ( x t | x t − 1 ) {\displaystyle P(x_{t}|x_{t-1})} ,
Simultaneous localization and mapping — P ( x t | o 1 : t , u 1 : t , m t ) = ∑ m t − 1 P ( o t | x t , m t , u 1 : t ) ∑ x t − 1 P ( x t | x t − 1 ) P ( x t − 1 | m t , o 1 : t − 1 , u 1 : t ) / Z {\displaystyle P(x_{t}|o_{1:t},u_{1:t},m_{t})=\sum _{m_{t-1}}P(o_{t}|x_{t},m_{t},u_{1:t})\sum _{x_{t-1}}P(x_{t}|x_{t-1})P(x_{t-1}|m_{t},o_{1:t-1},u_{1:t})/Z}
Simultaneous localization and mapping — P ( m t | x t , o 1 : t , u 1 : t ) = ∑ x t ∑ m t P ( m t | x t , m t − 1 , o t , u 1 : t ) P ( m t − 1 , x t | o 1 : t − 1 , m t − 1 , u 1 : t ) {\displaystyle P(m_{t}|x_{t},o_{1:t},u_{1:t})=\sum _{x_{t}}\sum _{m_{t}}P(m_{t}|x_{t},m_{t-1},o_{t},u_{1:t})P(m_{t-1},x_{t}|o_{1:t-1},m_{t-1},u_{1:t})}
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Like many inference problems, the solutions to inferring the two variables together can be found, to a local optimum solution, by alternating updates of the two beliefs in a form of an expectation–maximization algorithm.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — == Algorithms == Statistical techniques used to approximate the above equations include Kalman filters and particle filters (the algorithm behind Monte Carlo Localization).
Simultaneous localization and mapping — They provide an estimation of the posterior probability distribution for the pose of the robot and for the parameters of the map.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Methods which conservatively approximate the above model using covariance intersection are able to avoid reliance on statistical independence assumptions to reduce algorithmic complexity for large-scale applications.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Other approximation methods achieve improved computational efficiency by using simple bounded-region representations of uncertainty.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — They provide a set which encloses the pose of the robot and a set approximation of the map.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Bundle adjustment, and more generally maximum a posteriori estimation (MAP), is another popular technique for SLAM using image data, which jointly estimates poses and landmark positions, increasing map fidelity, and is used in commercialized SLAM systems such as Google's ARCore which replaces their prior augmented reality computing platform named Tango, formerly Project Tango.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — MAP estimators compute the most likely explanation of the robot poses and the map given the sensor data, rather than trying to estimate the entire posterior probability.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — New SLAM algorithms remain an active research area, and are often driven by differing requirements and assumptions about the types of maps, sensors and models as detailed below.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Many SLAM systems can be viewed as combinations of choices from each of these aspects.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Mapping === Topological maps are a method of environment representation which capture the connectivity (i.e., topology) of the environment rather than creating a geometrically accurate map.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Topological SLAM approaches have been used to enforce global consistency in metric SLAM algorithms.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — In contrast, grid maps use arrays (typically square or hexagonal) of discretized cells to represent a topological world, and make inferences about which cells are occupied.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Typically the cells are assumed to be statistically independent to simplify computation.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Under such assumption, P ( m t | x t , m t − 1 , o t ) {\displaystyle P(m_{t}|x_{t},m_{t-1},o_{t})} are set to 1 if the new map's cells are consistent with the observation o t {\displaystyle o_{t}} at location x t {\displaystyle x_{t}} and 0 if inconsistent.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Modern self driving cars mostly simplify the mapping problem to almost nothing, by making extensive use of highly detailed map data collected in advance.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — This can include map annotations to the level of marking locations of individual white line segments and curbs on the road.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Location-tagged visual data such as Google's StreetView may also be used as part of maps.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Essentially such systems simplify the SLAM problem to a simpler localization only task, perhaps allowing for moving objects such as cars and people only to be updated in the map at runtime.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — SLAM will always use several different types of sensors, and the powers and limits of various sensor types have been a major driver of new algorithms.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Statistical independence is the mandatory requirement to cope with metric bias and with noise in measurements.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Different types of sensors give rise to different SLAM algorithms which assumptions are most appropriate to the sensors.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — At one extreme, laser scans or visual features provide details of many points within an area, sometimes rendering SLAM inference unnecessary because shapes in these point clouds can be easily and unambiguously aligned at each step via image registration.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — At the opposite extreme, tactile sensors are extremely sparse as they contain only information about points very close to the agent, so they require strong prior models to compensate in purely tactile SLAM.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Most practical SLAM tasks fall somewhere between these visual and tactile extremes.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Landmarks are uniquely identifiable objects in the world which location can be estimated by a sensor, such as Wi-Fi access points or radio beacons.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Raw-data approaches make no assumption that landmarks can be identified, and instead model P ( o t | x t ) {\displaystyle P(o_{t}|x_{t})} directly as a function of the location.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Optical sensors may be one-dimensional (single beam) or 2D- (sweeping) laser rangefinders, 3D high definition light detection and ranging (lidar), 3D flash lidar, 2D or 3D sonar sensors, and one or more 2D cameras.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Since the invention of local features, such as SIFT, there has been intense research into visual SLAM (VSLAM) using primarily visual (camera) sensors, because of the increasing ubiquity of cameras such as those in mobile devices.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Both visual and lidar sensors are informative enough to allow for landmark extraction in many cases.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Other recent forms of SLAM include tactile SLAM (sensing by local touch only), radar SLAM, acoustic SLAM, and Wi-Fi-SLAM (sensing by strengths of nearby Wi-Fi access points).
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Recent approaches apply quasi-optical wireless ranging for multi-lateration (real-time locating system (RTLS)) or multi-angulation in conjunction with SLAM as a tribute to erratic wireless measures.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — A kind of SLAM for human pedestrians uses a shoe mounted inertial measurement unit as the main sensor and relies on the fact that pedestrians are able to avoid walls to automatically build floor plans of buildings by an indoor positioning system.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — For some outdoor applications, the need for SLAM has been almost entirely removed due to high precision differential GPS sensors.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — From a SLAM perspective, these may be viewed as location sensors which likelihoods are so sharp that they completely dominate the inference.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — However, GPS sensors may occasionally decline or go down entirely, e.g. during times of military conflict, which are of particular interest to some robotics applications.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Kinematics modeling === The P ( x t | x t − 1 ) {\displaystyle P(x_{t}|x_{t-1})} term represents the kinematics of the model, which usually include information about action commands given to a robot.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — As a part of the model, the kinematics of the robot is included, to improve estimates of sensing under conditions of inherent and ambient noise.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — The dynamic model balances the contributions from various sensors, various partial error models and finally comprises in a sharp virtual depiction as a map with the location and heading of the robot as some cloud of probability.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Mapping is the final depicting of such model, the map is either such depiction or the abstract term for the model.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — For 2D robots, the kinematics are usually given by a mixture of rotation and "move forward" commands, which are implemented with additional motor noise.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Unfortunately the distribution formed by independent noise in angular and linear directions is non-Gaussian, but is often approximated by a Gaussian.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — An alternative approach is to ignore the kinematic term and read odometry data from robot wheels after each command—such data may then be treated as one of the sensors rather than as kinematics.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Moving objects === Non-static environments, such as those containing other vehicles or pedestrians, continue to present research challenges.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — SLAM with DATMO is a model which tracks moving objects in a similar way to the agent itself.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Loop closure === Loop closure is the problem of recognizing a previously-visited location and updating beliefs accordingly.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — This can be a problem because model or algorithm errors can assign low priors to the location.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Typical loop closure methods apply a second algorithm to compute some type of sensor measure similarity, and reset the location priors when a match is detected.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — For example, this can be done by storing and comparing bag of words vectors of scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) features from each previously visited location.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Exploration === Active SLAM studies the combined problem of SLAM with deciding where to move next to build the map as efficiently as possible.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — The need for active exploration is especially pronounced in sparse sensing regimes such as tactile SLAM.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Active SLAM is generally performed by approximating the entropy of the map under hypothetical actions. "Multi agent SLAM" extends this problem to the case of multiple robots coordinating themselves to explore optimally.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Biological inspiration === In neuroscience, the hippocampus appears to be involved in SLAM-like computations, giving rise to place cells, and has formed the basis for bio-inspired SLAM systems such as RatSLAM.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Collaborative SLAM === Collaborative SLAM combines sensors from multiple robots or users to generate 3D maps.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — This capability was demonstrated by a number of teams in the 2021 DARPA Subterranean Challenge.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Acoustic SLAM === An extension of the common SLAM problem has been applied to the acoustic domain, where environments are represented by the three-dimensional (3D) position of sound sources, termed aSLAM (Acoustic Simultaneous Localization and Mapping).
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Early implementations of this technique have used direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimates of the sound source location, and rely on principal techniques of sound localization to determine source locations.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — An observer, or robot must be equipped with a microphone array to enable use of Acoustic SLAM, so that DoA features are properly estimated.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Acoustic SLAM has paved foundations for further studies in acoustic scene mapping, and can play an important role in human-robot interaction through speech.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — To map multiple, and occasionally intermittent sound sources, an acoustic SLAM system uses foundations in random finite set theory to handle the varying presence of acoustic landmarks.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — However, the nature of acoustically derived features leaves Acoustic SLAM susceptible to problems of reverberation, inactivity, and noise within an environment.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === Audiovisual SLAM === Originally designed for human–robot interaction, Audio-Visual SLAM is a framework that provides the fusion of landmark features obtained from both the acoustic and visual modalities within an environment.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Human interaction is characterized by features perceived in not only the visual modality, but the acoustic modality as well; as such, SLAM algorithms for human-centered robots and machines must account for both sets of features.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — An Audio-Visual framework estimates and maps positions of human landmarks through use of visual features like human pose, and audio features like human speech, and fuses the beliefs for a more robust map of the environment.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — For applications in mobile robotics (ex. drones, service robots), it is valuable to use low-power, lightweight equipment such as monocular cameras, or microelectronic microphone arrays.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Audio-Visual SLAM can also allow for complimentary function of such sensors, by compensating the narrow field-of-view, feature occlusions, and optical degradations common to lightweight visual sensors with the full field-of-view, and unobstructed feature representations inherent to audio sensors.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — The susceptibility of audio sensors to reverberation, sound source inactivity, and noise can also be accordingly compensated through fusion of landmark beliefs from the visual modality.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Complimentary function between the audio and visual modalities in an environment can prove valuable for the creation of robotics and machines that fully interact with human speech and human movement.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Various SLAM algorithms are implemented in the open-source software Robot Operating System (ROS) libraries, often used together with the Point Cloud Library for 3D maps or visual features from OpenCV.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === EKF SLAM === In robotics, EKF SLAM is a class of algorithms which uses the extended Kalman filter (EKF) for SLAM.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Typically, EKF SLAM algorithms are feature based, and use the maximum likelihood algorithm for data association.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — In the 1990s and 2000s, EKF SLAM had been the de facto method for SLAM, until the introduction of FastSLAM.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Associated with the EKF is the gaussian noise assumption, which significantly impairs EKF SLAM's ability to deal with uncertainty.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — With greater amount of uncertainty in the posterior, the linearization in the EKF fails.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — === GraphSLAM === In robotics, GraphSLAM is a SLAM algorithm which uses sparse information matrices produced by generating a factor graph of observation interdependencies (two observations are related if they contain data about the same landmark).
Simultaneous localization and mapping — == History == A seminal work in SLAM is the research of Smith and Cheeseman on the representation and estimation of spatial uncertainty in 1986.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Other pioneering work in this field was conducted by the research group of Hugh F.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Durrant-Whyte in the early 1990s. which showed that solutions to SLAM exist in the infinite data limit.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — This finding motivates the search for algorithms which are computationally tractable and approximate the solution.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — The acronym SLAM was coined within the paper, "Localization of Autonomous Guided Vehicles" which first appeared in ISR in 1995.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — The self-driving STANLEY and JUNIOR cars, led by Sebastian Thrun, won the DARPA Grand Challenge and came second in the DARPA Urban Challenge in the 2000s, and included SLAM systems, bringing SLAM to worldwide attention.
Simultaneous localization and mapping — Mass-market SLAM implementations can now be found in consumer robot vacuum cleaners and virtual reality headsets such as the Meta Quest 2 and PICO 4 for markerless inside-out tracking.

ARKit — ARKit is an application programming interface (API) for iOS, iPadOS and VisionOS which lets third-party developers build augmented reality apps, taking advantage of a device's camera, CPU, GPU, and motion sensors.
ARKit — The ARKit functionality is only available to users of devices with Apple A9 and later processors.
ARKit — According to Apple, this is because "these processors deliver breakthrough performance that enables fast scene understanding and lets you build detailed and compelling virtual content on top of real-world scenes." The SDK was first released for IOS 11 in 2017, and was preinstalled in the initial release of IPadOS 13 in 2019 and visionOS 1.0 in 2024.
ARKit — In visionOS, however, ARKit plays a lesser role in augmented reality than in iOS and iPadOS.
ARKit — ARKit in visionOS is focused on acquiring data about the person’s surroundings, while SwiftUI and RealityKit control the placement of any 2D or 3D content in the person’s surroundings, and SwiftUI or UIKit are used to build windows with an app's content.
ARKit — == See also == ARCore – Software development kit for building augmented reality applications OpenXR – Standard for access to virtual reality and augmented reality platforms and devices
ARCore — ARCore, also known as Google Play Services for AR, is a software development kit developed by Google that allows for augmented reality (AR) applications to be built.
ARCore — == Key technologies == ARCore uses a few key technologies to integrate virtual content with the real world as seen through the camera of a smartphone or tablet.
ARCore — Each of these technologies can be utilized by developers to create a high-quality, immersive AR experience.
ARCore — === Six degrees of freedom === Allows the phone to understand and track its position relative to the world.
ARCore — A motion tracking process known as simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) utilizes feature points - which are visually distinct objects within camera view - to provide focal points for the phone to determine proper positioning (pose) of the device.
ARCore — === Environmental understanding === Allows the phone to detect the size and location of flat surfaces - both vertical and horizontal - with feature points.
ARCore — A scene semantics API is used to gather real-time semantic data about the user's surroundings and uses that data to identify objects and features in view.
ARCore — === Light estimation === Lighting Estimation API allows the phone to estimate the environment's current lighting conditions and display images accurately in relation to real-world lighting.
ARCore — Lighting cues such as shadows and highlights are used to more immersively display virtual objects.
ARCore — === Depth analysis === Utilizes the phone's camera to create depth maps, which enable the device to more accurately determine the amount of space between surfaces based on what is captured.
ARCore — In order to properly assess the real world, depth maps are created to measure the amount of space between objects or surfaces.
ARCore — A depth-from-motion algorithm takes the motion data from the user's camera and utilizes it to create a more detailed depth map.
ARCore — === Geospatial capabilities === This function's API uses GPS and allows creators to give users unique experiences based on their real-world location.
ARCore — Matches the user's visual data with that of Google Maps to determine precise location.
ARCore — == See also == ARKit – Augmented reality API for Apple platforms OpenXR – Standard for access to virtual reality and augmented reality platforms and devices
D3.js — D3.js (also known as D3, short for Data-Driven Documents) is a JavaScript library for producing dynamic, interactive data visualizations in web browsers.
D3.js — It makes use of Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG), HTML5, and Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) standards.
D3.js — Its development was noted in 2011, as version 2.0.0 was released in August 2011.
D3.js — With the release of version 4.0.0 in June 2016, D3 was changed from a single library into a collection of smaller, modular libraries that can be used independently.
D3.js — == Context == There have been various previous attempts to bring data visualization to web browsers.
D3.js — The most notable examples were the Prefuse, Flare, and Protovis toolkits, which can all be considered as direct predecessors of D3.js.
D3.js — Prefuse was a visualization toolkit created in 2005 that required usage of Java, and visualizations were rendered within browsers with a Java plug-in.
D3.js — Flare was a similar toolkit from 2007 that used ActionScript, and required a Flash plug-in for rendering.
D3.js — In 2009, based on the experience of developing and utilizing Prefuse and Flare, Jeffrey Heer, Mike Bostock, and Vadim Ogievetsky of Stanford University's Stanford Visualization Group created Protovis, a JavaScript library to generate SVG graphics from data.
D3.js — In 2011, the development of Protovis was stopped to focus on a new project, D3.js.
D3.js — Informed by experiences with Protovis, Bostock, along with Heer and Ogievetsky, developed D3.js to provide a more expressive framework that, at the same time, focuses on web standards and provides improved performance.
D3.js — == Technical principles == The D3.js library uses pre-built functions to select elements, create SVG objects, style them, or add transitions, dynamic effects, or tooltips.
D3.js — Large datasets can be bound to SVG objects using D3.js functions to generate text/graphic charts and diagrams.
D3.js — The data can be in various formats such as JSON, comma-separated values (CSV) or geoJSON, but, if required, JavaScript functions can be written to read other data formats.
D3.js — === Selections === The central principle of D3.js design is to enable the programmer to first use a CSS-style selector to select a given set of Document Object Model (DOM) nodes, then use operators to manipulate them in a similar manner to jQuery.
D3.js — For example, one may select all HTML paragraph elements (represented by <p>...</p>), and then change their text color, e.g. to lavender:
D3.js — The selection can be based on an HTML tag, class, identifier, attribute, or place in the hierarchy.
D3.js — This includes getting and setting attributes, display texts, and styles (as in the above example).
D3.js — This process of modifying, creating and removing HTML elements can be made dependent on data, which is the basic concept of D3.js.
D3.js — === Transitions === By declaring a transition, values for attributes and styles can be smoothly interpolated over a certain time.
D3.js — The following code will make all HTML <p>...</p> elements on a page gradually change their text color to pink:
D3.js — === Data-binding === For more advanced uses, loaded data drives the creation of elements.
D3.js — D3.js loads a given dataset, then, for each of its elements, creates an SVG object with associated properties (shape, colors, values) and behaviors (transitions, events).
D3.js — === Appending nodes using data === Once a dataset is bound to a document, use of D3.js typically follows a pattern wherein an explicit .enter() function, an implicit "update," and an explicit .exit() function is invoked for each item in the bound dataset.
D3.js — Any methods chained after the .enter() command will be called for each item in the dataset not already represented by a DOM node in the selection (the previous selectAll()).
D3.js — Likewise, the implicit update function is called on all existing selected nodes for which there is a corresponding item in the dataset, and .exit() is called on all existing selected nodes that do not have an item in the dataset to bind to them.
D3.js — == Community == D3.js is a popular toolset used by many individuals and organizations for data visualization.
D3.js — Mike Bostock created bl.ocks as a website for sharing D3 visualizations and code snippets, which used GitHub Gist to host the code.
D3.js — He later created Observable as a place where programmers could make and share visualizations. (Similar to bl.ocks but the code is all hosted on the observable site).
